definition: Information gathered with the senses or instruments, without interpretation. Example: 'the liquid fizzed'.
An observation expressed as a number with a unit and an uncertainty, made by comparison with a standard.
A testable, tentative explanation or prediction. Data can support or contradict it; it is never 'proved' by a single experiment.
A simplified representation of a system (a diagram, equation or simulation) used to explain and predict. Every model has limitations.
A well-tested, broadly accepted explanation of many observations, supported by a large body of evidence (for example atomic theory). Not a guess.
A concise statement, often an equation, describing a regularity in nature (for example conservation of mass). Laws describe; theories explain.
The variable you deliberately change in an experiment.
The variable you measure to see the effect of changing the independent variable.
A variable kept constant so it cannot affect the result.
The range within which the true value is expected to lie. A result is meaningless without some idea of its uncertainty.
The digits in a number that carry meaningful information about its precision.
How close a measurement is to the true value.
How close repeated measurements are to each other, or how finely an instrument can resolve a value.
A substance made of only one kind of atom (all atoms with the same number of protons).
A substance made of two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, with properties different from its elements.
Two or more substances physically combined; each keeps its own properties and they can be separated by physical means.
A homogeneous mixture in which a solute is dissolved in a solvent.
A mixture of a metal with other elements (for example steel, bronze, brass).
A naturally occurring, inorganic, crystalline solid with a definite chemical composition range.
Rock containing enough of a valuable mineral to be extracted profitably.
The smallest unit of an element, made of a nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different mass numbers.
An atom or group of atoms with an electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons.
The SI unit of amount of substance: exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ particles.
The mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol.
A process in which substances are transformed into different substances by rearranging atoms.
A change in state, shape or mixing that does not produce a new substance (melting, dissolving, grinding).
Releasing energy to the surroundings (ΔH negative).
Absorbing energy from the surroundings (ΔH positive).
A substance that donates hydrogen ions (H⁺) in solution (Brønsted–Lowry definition).
A substance that accepts hydrogen ions; soluble bases (alkalis) produce OH⁻ in water.
A logarithmic measure of acidity: pH ≈ −log₁₀[H⁺]. Each unit is a tenfold change.
A substance whose colour depends on pH over a characteristic range.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
Using electric current to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.
Mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V.
A push or pull, measured in newtons (N). A vector quantity.
A quantity with magnitude only (mass, speed, energy).
A quantity with magnitude and direction (velocity, force, momentum).
The capacity to do work or transfer heat, measured in joules (J). It is conserved.
The rate of transferring energy, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s).
Useful energy output divided by total energy input; always less than 100 % in real machines.
A measure of the average kinetic energy of particles. Absolute zero is 0 K (−273.15 °C).
Energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
Energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g (or 1 kg) of a substance by 1 K.
Energy absorbed or released during a change of state at constant temperature.
How well a material conducts heat, in W/(m·K).
Potential difference: energy transferred per unit charge, in volts (1 V = 1 J/C).
Rate of flow of electric charge, in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s).
Opposition to current, R = V/I, in ohms (Ω).
Components connected one after another, so the same current flows through each.
Components connected across the same two points, so each has the same voltage.
The energy per unit charge supplied by a source such as a battery (EMF), in volts.
The change in direction of light as it crosses a boundary between materials with different refractive indices.
The ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to its speed in a material.
The distance from a lens to the point where parallel rays converge.
Separation of white light into colours because the refractive index depends on wavelength.
The set of wavelengths emitted by excited atoms; unique for each element.
